questions.stem: Which one of the following CPU scheduling algorithms cannot be preemptive?

steps.title: What preemptive means, and the one test
steps.body: The CPU scheduler picks one ready process and lets it run. A policy is **preemptive** if the scheduler may take the CPU away from a running process before that process finishes its CPU burst, and hand it to another ready process. A policy is **non-preemptive** if a running process keeps the CPU until its burst ends or it blocks. The test for "can this policy be preemptive": does the policy have a ranking (or a timer) under which a ready process can beat the one that is running? If a newcomer can outrank the running process, or the running process can use up a time limit, a preemptive version exists. If no newcomer can ever outrank the running process, the policy has no preemptive version.

steps.title: SRTF, Round Robin and Priority each have a way to displace the running process
steps.body: SRTF ranks by remaining burst time. Run a process of burst 3 for 1 unit, so 2 remain; a newcomer with burst 1 has smaller remaining time and takes the CPU. SRTF is in fact SJF made preemptive. Round Robin ranks nobody; it uses a timer: after a quantum expires the running process goes to the back of the queue even if it still needs CPU. Priority scheduling ranks by a priority number; when a process of better priority arrives, the preemptive form hands it the CPU at once (the non-preemptive form waits for the burst to end, so priority has both forms).

steps.title: FCFS ranks by arrival time, and no newcomer can win that ranking
steps.body: FCFS serves processes in order of arrival. The running process arrived earlier than everything waiting behind it, and every future arrival is later still. So no ready process ever ranks above the running one, and there is no moment at which a rule would take the CPU away. FCFS can only be non-preemptive. A script that searches small scenarios confirms it: a newcomer can outrank the running process under SRTF and under Priority, never under FCFS. The answer is FCFS, option B.

shortcut.body: Read the word "cannot" and look for the policy with no preemptive form. Each policy decides by something that can change while a process runs: remaining time (SRTF), the quantum timer (RR), priority (both forms). FCFS decides by arrival time, which never favours a newcomer. About 20 seconds. This works because the four names are standard; a policy invented in the stem would need the ranking test from step 1.

traps.text: SRTF is not a separate idea from SJF; it is SJF with preemption added. Picking it because "shortest job first" sounds non-preemptive confuses the two versions.

Round Robin is described as FCFS plus a quantum, which makes some candidates carry FCFS's non-preemption over to it. The quantum is exactly the preemption: when the timer expires the running process is removed.

Priority scheduling comes in two forms. A question that asks for the policy that cannot be preemptive needs one with no preemptive form at all; priority has one (a higher-priority arrival takes the CPU).

recognize.clues: The stem asks which algorithm "cannot be preemptive", so the question is about the preemptive versus non-preemptive split, and the test is whether a newcomer or a timer can displace the running process.
recognize.contrast: Do not confuse this with a question about which policy is optimal for waiting time or which can starve a process; those concern fairness and averages, not whether the running process can be interrupted.

check.body: Take two processes with FCFS: P1 arrives at 0 with burst 5, P2 arrives at 1 with burst 1. P2 waits until time 5 whatever its burst, because P1 is ahead of it by arrival. Run the same two under SRTF and P2 takes the CPU at time 1. Only FCFS refuses to let P2 in.

questions.stem: Consider a CPU that has to execute two types of processes. The first type, Actuators (A), requires a CPU burst of 6 seconds. The second type, Controllers (C), requires a CPU burst of 8 seconds. A new process of type A arrives at time $t = 10, 20, 30, 40$, and $50$ (in seconds). Similarly, a new process of type C arrives at time $t = 11, 22, 33, 44$, and $55$ (in seconds). The CPU scheduling policy is First Come First Serve (FCFS). The first process of type A starts running at $t = 10$ seconds. The average waiting time (in seconds) for the 10 processes is ___________. (rounded off to one decimal place)

solutionDiagram.alt: FCFS Gantt chart for the ten processes: A1 from 10 to 16, C1 16 to 24, A2 24 to 30, C2 30 to 38, A3 38 to 44, C3 44 to 52, A4 52 to 58, C4 58 to 66, A5 66 to 72, C5 72 to 80, with each arrival marked above.

steps.title: Waiting time and the FCFS rule
steps.body: A process has an **arrival time** (when it enters the ready queue) and a **CPU burst** (how long it needs the CPU). Its **waiting time** is the time it sits in the ready queue: with one burst and no I/O, that is start time minus arrival time. **FCFS** means first come, first served: the CPU is given to the process that arrived earliest, and it keeps the CPU until its burst ends. So each process starts at the later of its own arrival time and the moment the previous process finishes.

steps.title: Put the ten processes in arrival order
steps.body: Merge the two arrival lists. Type A has burst 6 and arrives at 10, 20, 30, 40, 50; type C has burst 8 and arrives at 11, 22, 33, 44, 55. In order of arrival the queue is A1 (10), C1 (11), A2 (20), C2 (22), A3 (30), C3 (33), A4 (40), C4 (44), A5 (50), C5 (55). The question tells us the first process, A1, starts at 10.

steps.title: Run the schedule, one process at a time
steps.body: A1 starts 10, ends 16, waits 0. C1 arrived at 11, starts 16, ends 24, waits 5. A2 arrived at 20, starts 24, ends 30, waits 4. C2 arrived at 22, starts 30, ends 38, waits 8. A3 arrived at 30, starts 38, ends 44, waits 8. C3 arrived at 33, starts 44, ends 52, waits 11. A4 arrived at 40, starts 52, ends 58, waits 12. C4 arrived at 44, starts 58, ends 66, waits 14. A5 arrived at 50, starts 66, ends 72, waits 16. C5 arrived at 55, starts 72, ends 80, waits 17. Every process arrives before the previous one ends, so the CPU is never idle after time 10 and each start equals the previous finish.

steps.title: Add the waits and divide by ten
steps.body: The waits are 0, 5, 4, 8, 8, 11, 12, 14, 16, 17, which sum to 95. The mean over 10 processes is 9.5 seconds, already one decimal place.

shortcut.body: The CPU never idles after 10, so the starts are 10 plus running totals of the bursts taken in arrival order A, C, A, C, ...: 10, 16, 24, 30, 38, 44, 52, 58, 66, 72, which sum to 410. The arrivals sum to $150 + 165 = 315$. The total wait is the difference, 95, and the mean is 9.5. Unsafe if the CPU can sit idle (a start would then be an arrival, not a previous finish).

traps.text: Reporting the turnaround time instead of the waiting time gives 16.5 (the mean burst, 7, is added to every wait). The question asks for waiting.
Averaging start times rather than start minus arrival gives 41.0. A start time is a clock reading; the wait is measured from the arrival.
Ordering by burst length (all Actuators first, as a shortest-job-first scheduler would) gives 8.7. The policy in the stem is FCFS, so arrival order decides.

recognize.clues: The stem names First Come First Serve outright and gives fixed arrival times with fixed bursts for two process types, so the schedule is just the arrival order with each start taken from the previous finish.
recognize.contrast: Shortest job first would reorder the A and C processes by burst length. Here the policy is stated as FCFS, so the order is the merged arrival order and the burst sizes only decide how long each one holds the CPU.

check.body: Go through turnaround instead. The finish times are 16, 24, 30, 38, 44, 52, 58, 66, 72 and 80, which sum to 480, and the arrivals sum to 315, so the mean turnaround is 165 / 10 = 16.5. The mean burst is (5 times 6 + 5 times 8) / 10 = 7. Waiting equals turnaround minus burst, and 16.5 minus 7 gives the same mean wait.

questions.stem:
Processes $P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4$ arrive in that order at times 0, 1, 2, and 8 milliseconds respectively, and have execution times of 10, 13, 6, and 9 milliseconds respectively. Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) algorithm is used as the CPU scheduling policy. Ignore context switching times.

Which ONE of the following correctly gives the average turnaround time of the four processes in milliseconds?

solutionDiagram.alt: SRTF Gantt chart: P1 runs 0 to 2, P3 2 to 8, P1 8 to 16, P4 16 to 25, P2 25 to 38, with the arrivals of P1 at 0, P2 at 1, P3 at 2 and P4 at 8 marked.

steps.title: Turnaround time and the SRTF rule
steps.body: **Turnaround time** is completion time minus arrival time: how long a process spends in the system from arrival to finish. **Remaining time** is burst minus the time already executed. **SRTF** is the preemptive form of shortest job first: whenever a process arrives or finishes, the scheduler runs the ready process with the smallest remaining time, so a newcomer whose burst is shorter than what the running process still needs takes the CPU. Context switching costs nothing here.

steps.title: Follow the events in time order
steps.body: t = 0: only P1 is present, so P1 runs. t = 1: P2 arrives with 13, but P1 has 9 left, so P1 continues. t = 2: P3 arrives with 6, and P1 has 8 left, so P3 preempts and runs 2 to 8. t = 8: P3 finishes. P4 arrives at the same moment with 9. Ready: P1 with 8 left, P2 with 13, P4 with 9. P1 is smallest and runs 8 to 16. t = 16: P4 (9) beats P2 (13), so P4 runs 16 to 25. Last, P2 runs 25 to 38.

steps.title: Completion and turnaround of each process
steps.body: P1 completes at 16, so its turnaround is 16 - 0 = 16. P2 completes at 38: 38 - 1 = 37. P3 completes at 8: 8 - 2 = 6. P4 completes at 25: 25 - 8 = 17.

steps.title: Average turnaround time
steps.body: The sum is 16 + 37 + 6 + 17 = 76, and 76 / 4 = 19 ms. This is option D.

shortcut.body: Draw the five-segment Gantt chart (the decisions are at t = 1, 2, 8 and 16). The completion times are 8, 16, 25, 38, and a turnaround is a completion minus that process's arrival. About 2.5 minutes. A sanity check: the CPU is busy from 0 to 38 (total burst 38), so the last completion must be 38.

traps.text: 22 is what comes out of the wrong policy or the wrong quantity: FCFS gives a mean turnaround of 22.25, and the mean of the completion times (8, 16, 25, 38) is 21.75. Both round to 22.
15 cannot be right for any schedule. Mean turnaround equals mean waiting time plus mean burst (9.5), and SRTF already gives the smallest possible mean waiting time, 9.5, so no schedule goes below 19.
37 is the turnaround of P2 alone, the largest of the four. The question asks for the average of all four.

recognize.clues: The stem names Shortest Remaining Time First and gives arrivals at different times with ignored switching cost, so the schedule must be rebuilt at each arrival by comparing remaining times.
recognize.contrast: Non-preemptive shortest job first would let P1 run to 10 before choosing. Here P3 arrives at 2 and can displace P1, which is the difference to watch for in an SRTF question.

check.body: Add up what each process actually ran. P1 runs 0 to 2 and 8 to 16, which is 10 ms. P3 runs 2 to 8, which is 6 ms. P4 runs 16 to 25, which is 9 ms. P2 runs 25 to 38, which is 13 ms. Every total matches its burst, and the five segments tile 0 to 38 with no gap, so the completion times are consistent.

questions.stem:
A computer has two processors, $M_1$ and $M_2$. Four processes $P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4$ with CPU bursts of 20, 16, 25, and 10 milliseconds, respectively, arrive at the same time and these are the only processes in the system. The scheduler uses non-preemptive priority scheduling, with priorities decided as follows:

- $M_1$ uses priority of execution for the processes as, $P_1 > P_3 > P_2 > P_4$, i.e., $P_1$ and $P_4$ have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.
- $M_2$ uses priority of execution for the processes as, $P_2 > P_3 > P_4 > P_1$, i.e., $P_2$ and $P_1$ have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.

A process $P_i$ is scheduled to a processor $M_k$, if the processor is free and no other process $P_j$ is waiting with higher priority. At any given point of time, a process can be allocated to any one of the free processors without violating the execution priority rules. Ignore the context switch time. What will be the average waiting time of the processes in milliseconds?

solutionDiagram.alt: Gantt chart for two processors: M1 runs P1 from 0 to 20 then P4 from 20 to 30; M2 runs P2 from 0 to 16 then P3 from 16 to 41.

steps.title: Waiting time, non-preemptive, and priority per processor
steps.body: **Waiting time** is the time a process spends ready but not running; every process here arrives at 0, so its waiting time is the moment it starts. **Non-preemptive** means a started process runs to the end of its burst. With two processors, each one is a separate server. The rule in the stem: when a processor becomes free, it takes the waiting process that ranks highest in its own priority list, and it never starts a lower-ranked process while a higher-ranked one is waiting.

steps.title: Time 0: both processors are free and all four processes wait
steps.body: M1 ranks P1 first, so it starts P1 (20 ms, ends at 20). M2 ranks P2 first, so it starts P2 (16 ms, ends at 16). The two top choices differ, so there is no conflict. P1 and P2 each wait 0.

steps.title: Time 16: M2 frees first
steps.body: P2 ends at 16. Waiting: P3 and P4. M2's order is P2 > P3 > P4 > P1, so P3 beats P4. M2 starts P3 at 16 (25 ms, ends at 41). P3 waited 16.

steps.title: Time 20: M1 frees, only P4 is left
steps.body: P1 ends at 20. The only waiting process is P4, so M1 starts it at 20. P4 waited 20. Total waiting = 0 + 0 + 16 + 20 = 36 ms, and the mean over four processes is 9.00 ms, option A.

shortcut.body: Each processor takes its own top choice at time 0 (P1 and P2); after that the choices are forced: M2 frees at 16 and picks P3 over P4, then M1 frees at 20 and takes P4. Waits 16 and 20 give 36 / 4 = 9. About 1.5 minutes. Elimination does not help much because the other three values come from schedules that look reasonable but break the priority rule.

traps.text: 8.75 is the mean wait of schedules such as P3 then P1 on one processor against P4 then P2 on the other. Every schedule with a mean of 8.75, 7.50 or 6.50 (checked by listing all 384 orders and processor splits) starts P4 at time 0, which the priority lists forbid.

6.50 is the best mean wait any two-processor schedule can reach, by running short jobs first. It ignores the priority lists: at time 0 neither processor would pick P4 while higher-ranked processes wait.
7.50 comes from schedules that again start P4 at time 0 (for example P1 then P2 on one machine against P4 then P3 on the other). That starts P4 while higher-ranked processes are still waiting.

recognize.clues: The stem says non-preemptive priority scheduling and gives a ranking for each processor, so every decision is a lookup of the best waiting process in that processor's list.
recognize.contrast: Do not treat it as shortest job first. The bursts only set how long a processor stays busy; the choice of who starts next comes from the priority lists, not from the burst lengths.

check.body: Recompute the waits from the finish times instead of the start times. Waiting time is completion minus burst. On M1, the first process ends at 20 and the fourth at 30 (20 + 10). On M2, the second ends at 16 and the third at 41 (16 + 25). Waits: 20 - 20 = 0, 16 - 16 = 0, 41 - 25 = 16, 30 - 10 = 20. The sum is 36 and 36 / 4 = 9.00, matching the start-time sum.

questions.stem:
Consider a single processor system with four processes A, B, C, and D, represented as given below, where for each process the first value is its arrival time, and the second value is its CPU burst time.

A (0, 10), B (2, 6), C (4, 3), and D (6, 7).

Which one of the following options gives the average waiting times when preemptive Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) and Non-Preemptive Shortest Job First (NP-SJF) CPU scheduling algorithms are applied to the processes?

solutionDiagram.alt: Two Gantt charts. SRTF: A 0 to 2, B 2 to 4, C 4 to 7, B 7 to 11, D 11 to 18, A 18 to 26. Non-preemptive SJF: A 0 to 10, C 10 to 13, B 13 to 19, D 19 to 26.

steps.title: Waiting time, SRTF and NP-SJF
steps.body: **Waiting time** is the time spent ready but not running: completion minus arrival minus burst. **Non-preemptive SJF** picks, each time the CPU frees up, the ready process with the shortest burst, and lets it finish. **SRTF** is the preemptive version: at every arrival the scheduler compares the newcomer's burst with the running process's remaining time and switches if the newcomer is shorter. Each algorithm gives its own schedule, so compute both.

steps.title: SRTF timeline
steps.body: t = 0: A runs. t = 2: B arrives with 6; A has 8 left, so B runs. t = 4: C arrives with 3; B has 4 left, so C runs. t = 6: D arrives with 7, but C has 1 left and continues. C ends at 7. Ready: A with 8, B with 4, D with 7, so B runs 7 to 11, then D 11 to 18, then A 18 to 26. Completion: A 26, B 11, C 7, D 18. Waits: A 26-0-10 = 16, B 11-2-6 = 3, C 7-4-3 = 0, D 18-6-7 = 5. Sum 24, mean 6.

steps.title: NP-SJF timeline
steps.body: At t = 0 only A is present, so A runs 0 to 10 with no interruption. At t = 10, B (6), C (3) and D (7) are all waiting. The shortest is C: 10 to 13. Then B (6) against D (7): B runs 13 to 19. D runs 19 to 26. Waits: A 0, C 10-4 = 6, B 13-2 = 11, D 19-6 = 13. Sum 30, mean 7.5.

steps.title: Match the pair to an option
steps.body: SRTF = 6 and NP-SJF = 7.5 is option B.

shortcut.body: NP-SJF takes four short lines (A, then C, B, D) and gives 7.5, which already leaves only B and C. Then settle SRTF with one number: A is the only process preempted for a long time, and its wait is 26 - 10 = 16; B waits 3 (it loses the CPU to C for 3), C 0, D 5. The total 24 gives 6, so B. About 2.5 minutes.

traps.text: NP-SJF = 7 is impossible. After A finishes, the six orders of B, C and D give mean waits of 7.5, 7.75, 8.25, 8.75, 9.25 and 9.5, and 7 is not among them.
SRTF = 7 would need a total wait of 28, but SRTF produces 24 here, and no schedule beats SRTF on mean waiting time. Recount the waits of A (16) and B (3) before trusting a larger figure.
Neither number holds: 8.5 is not the NP-SJF mean for any order of B, C, D after A (the listed means are 7.5, 7.75, 8.25, 8.75, 9.25, 9.5), and SRTF is 6, not 7.

recognize.clues: The stem asks for the same average under preemptive SRTF and non-preemptive SJF on one set of arrivals and bursts, which are the two forms of the shortest-job rule.
recognize.contrast: The two forms give different schedules. The test is whether a short late arrival may cut in on a running job; only SRTF allows it.

check.body: Both schedules keep the CPU busy from 0 to 26, so both last completions are 26 and the totals of waiting differ only through the other completion times. The SRTF completions are 26, 11, 7 and 18, summing to 62. The non-preemptive ones are 10, 19, 13 and 26, summing to 68. A gap of 6 in total completion is a gap of 6 in total wait, which is 4 times the gap between the two means.

questions.stem: Which one or more of the following CPU scheduling algorithms can potentially cause starvation?

steps.title: What starvation is, and the test for it
steps.body: **Starvation** (indefinite blocking) means a process is ready to run but never gets the CPU, because the scheduler keeps choosing other processes. A policy can starve a process only when its choice rule can keep ranking that process behind a never-ending supply of newcomers. So ask of each policy: what does it compare, and can newcomers keep winning the comparison? If the comparison is arrival order or turn order, the wait is bounded by a finite number of earlier processes. If it is a property such as priority or burst length, a stream of better newcomers can postpone a worse process forever.

steps.title: First-in First-out and Round Robin give a bounded wait
steps.body: Under FIFO a process waits only for those that arrived before it. That is a finite set, and each of them finishes after a finite burst, so the wait is bounded. Under Round Robin with $n$ ready processes and quantum $q$, a ready process gets the CPU within one cycle, at most $(n-1)q$ time units. Neither rule lets a newcomer jump ahead of a waiting process. A simulation with a steady stream of short higher-ranked arrivals agrees: the victim process of burst 20 finishes at time 21 under FIFO and at 61 under Round Robin.

steps.title: Priority and Shortest Job First can starve
steps.body: Priority scheduling always picks the best-priority ready process. If better-priority processes keep arriving, a low-priority process never reaches the front. This is the classic case, and aging (raising the priority of a waiting process over time) is the cure. Shortest Job First always picks the shortest burst, so a long job is passed over as long as shorter jobs keep arriving. In the same simulation (one new job of burst 1 every time unit) the victim never runs within 10000 time units under both policies. The answer is C and D.

shortcut.body: Starvation needs a policy that ranks by something a newcomer can beat: priority or job length. FIFO ranks by arrival and RR by turn, so neither starves. Mark C and D in about 30 seconds. FIFO is the one borderline case: a process that never ends would hold the CPU forever under a non-preemptive FIFO, and the key accepts both C and D alone and A, C and D together.

traps.text: FIFO does not starve a process by its own rule: every wait is bounded by the earlier arrivals. The only way to block others forever is a process with an infinite burst, a fault of the process rather than of the policy, and the official key scored both {C, D} and {A, C, D}.
Round Robin is sometimes marked because a long job needs many turns. It is slow, not starved: every ready process gets a quantum in each cycle, so the wait for a turn is at most $(n-1)q$.
Leaving Priority Scheduling out is the commonest loss of marks. Without aging, a steady supply of higher-priority arrivals keeps a low-priority process in the ready queue for ever.
Shortest Job First is optimal for mean waiting time, which tempts candidates to call it fair. The optimality is exactly what starves long jobs when short ones keep coming.

recognize.clues: The phrase "can potentially cause starvation" asks about the ranking rule of each policy and whether newcomers can keep outranking a waiting process indefinitely.
recognize.contrast: Starvation is different from a long average wait. A policy with a bounded wait for every process can still be slow, but it does not starve anyone.

check.body: Test each policy on a concrete stream. One victim job of burst 10 arrives at time 0, and a new job of burst 1 arrives at every time unit. If the new jobs rank higher, the victim never runs under the policy that ranks by priority and under the one that ranks by remaining time. Under first come first served the victim is first in line and runs at time 0, and under round robin it gets a turn within one cycle.

questions.stem: Consider four processes P, Q, R, and S scheduled on a CPU as per round robin algorithm with a time quantum of 4 units. The processes arrive in the order P, Q, R, S, all at time $t = 0$. There is exactly one context switch from S to Q, exactly one context switch from R to Q, and exactly two context switches from Q to R. There is no context switch from S to P. Switching to a ready process after the termination of another process is also considered a context switch. Which one of the following is NOT possible as CPU burst time (in time units) of these processes?

solutionDiagram.alt: Four round robin Gantt charts with quantum 4, one per option. Options A, B and C run in the order P, Q, R, S, Q, R, Q. Option D runs P 0 to 3, Q 3 to 7, R 7 to 11, S 11 to 14, Q 14 to 17, R 17 to 20 and ends without a switch from R to Q.

steps.title: Round robin and what counts as a context switch
steps.body: Round robin keeps the ready processes in a first-in-first-out queue. The CPU is given to the process at the head for at most one **quantum** (here 4 units). If the process still needs CPU after its quantum, it goes to the back of the queue; if it finishes, it leaves. A **context switch X to Y** happens when the CPU passes from one process X to a different process Y. This includes the hand-over after X terminates, as the stem says. A process that continues alone (nobody else is ready) does not switch. All four processes arrive at 0, so the first round is P, Q, R, S.

steps.title: P must end in round one
steps.body: "No switch from S to P" says that right after S's turn, P is not waiting. P had its first turn at the start of round one, so it must have finished then: $P \le 4$. P to Q is then the first switch, and the CPU moves on through Q, R and S.

steps.title: What the counts force on Q and R, and S
steps.body: Q's first turn is followed by R, which is the first Q to R switch. A second Q to R needs a second Q turn, and R still waiting behind it: $Q > 4$ and $R > 4$. The one R to Q switch has to come after R's second turn (its first is followed by S), so Q is still alive after two turns: $Q > 8$. If R needed a third turn ($R > 8$), Q's third turn would end with a third Q to R, which the count forbids, so $4 < R \le 8$. After R ends, Q runs alone and no switch is added, so Q has no upper limit. For S, one S to Q switch is the hand-over at the end of round one, so S must not need a second turn: $S \le 4$. The turn order is P Q R S Q R Q. A script that tries every burst combination from 1 to 17 finds 576 satisfying sets, exactly those with these four limits.

steps.title: Test the four options
steps.body: A: P = 4, S = 2, R = 6, Q = 10 meets all four limits. B: P = 2, S = 1, R = 5, Q = 9 meets them. C: P = 4, S = 4, R = 5, Q = 12 meets them (Q's third turn ends exactly at its burst). D: P = 3, S = 3 and R = 7 are fine, but Q = 7 is not above 8. Q finishes in its second turn (4 + 3), so when R ends its second turn there is nobody to switch to, and the required R to Q switch never occurs. D is not possible: option D.

shortcut.body: Only the processes that must outlive two quanta matter: the turn order P Q R S Q R Q needs $Q > 8$ and $4 < R \le 8$, with P and S at most 4. All four options pass the P, S and R tests, so scan Q: 10, 9, 12 and 7, and only D has $Q \le 8$. About 2 minutes. Unsafe if you skip the check that P and S end in round one, because then a different order appears.

traps.text: Q = 10 and R = 6 look ragged next to a quantum of 4, but R only needs 2 units in its second turn and Q 2 units in its third. The counts come out right (see the chart for A).
S = 1 and P = 2 end well inside a quantum. The switch from S to Q still counts, because the stem says switching to a ready process after a termination is a context switch.
Q = 12 ends exactly at a quantum boundary (4, 4, 4) and S = 4 fills its quantum exactly. Candidates fear an extra switch there, but when Q is last it simply continues alone, so no switch is added.

recognize.clues: The stem gives a time quantum, simultaneous arrivals in a fixed order and counts of particular switches, so the question is about the turn sequence that round robin produces.
recognize.contrast: This is not a Gantt average-wait question. Nothing is averaged; the switch counts are used backwards to bound each burst, and the answer is the option that breaks a bound.

check.body: Simulate option C directly with a quantum of 4 and bursts P = 4, Q = 12, R = 5, S = 4. The turns run P, Q, R, S, Q, R, Q. That gives S to Q once, R to Q once, Q to R twice and S to P never, matching every count. Option D, with bursts 3, 7, 7, 3, runs P, Q, R, S, Q, R and stops, so R to Q never occurs.

questions.stem: Three processes arrive at time zero with CPU bursts of 16, 20 and 10 milliseconds. If the scheduler has prior knowledge about the length of the CPU bursts, the minimum achievable average waiting time for these three processes in a non-preemptive scheduler (rounded to nearest integer) is ___________ milliseconds.

solutionDiagram.alt: Gantt chart of shortest job first with all three processes arriving at 0: the 10 ms process runs 0 to 10, the 16 ms process runs 10 to 26, the 20 ms process runs 26 to 46.

steps.title: Waiting time and why shortest first is the minimum
steps.body: A process's **waiting time** is the time it sits in the ready queue; when all arrive at 0 it is the moment the process starts. **Non-preemptive** means a started process runs to the end of its burst. In a non-preemptive schedule the process in position $k$ delays every process after it by its own burst, so the first job's burst is counted in the wait of $n-1$ processes, the second's in $n-2$, and so on. To make the total small, give the largest counts to the smallest bursts: run **shortest job first**. Knowing the burst lengths in advance, as the stem says, is what lets the scheduler do this.

steps.title: Order the bursts and compute each start
steps.body: Sorted bursts: 10, 16, 20. The 10 ms process starts at 0 and waits 0. The 16 ms process starts at 10 and waits 10. The 20 ms process starts at 10 + 16 = 26 and waits 26.

steps.title: Average
steps.body: The total wait is 0 + 10 + 26 = 36, and 36 / 3 = 12 ms. It is already an integer, so rounding changes nothing. As a check, all six orders give means of 17.33, 14, 18.67, 16.67, 12 and 13.33; only SJF order reaches 12, the minimum.

shortcut.body: Sort the bursts $a \le b \le c$ and use $\text{total wait} = 2a + b$, since $a$ delays two processes and $b$ delays one and $c$ delays none. Here $2 \times 10 + 16 = 36$ and $36 / 3 = 12$. About 40 seconds. It holds for three processes that all arrive together.

traps.text: Running the processes in the order given (16, 20, 10) is FCFS, not the minimum: it gives 17.33, which rounds to 17.
Running the longest first (20, 16, 10) gives the maximum, 18.67, which rounds to 19.
Stopping at the total wait, 36, and not dividing by the three processes. The question asks for the average.

recognize.clues: The words "minimum achievable average waiting time" with prior knowledge of burst lengths and a non-preemptive scheduler point to shortest job first, which is optimal for average wait.
recognize.contrast: Do not reach for FCFS or round robin here. They fix the order without looking at burst lengths, so they only match the minimum by luck.

check.body: Use turnaround as a second route. In sorted order the completions are 10, 26 and 46, which sum to 82, so the mean turnaround is 82 / 3. The mean burst is 46 / 3. Waiting is turnaround minus burst, and (82 - 46) / 3 gives 12 again.

questions.stem:
Consider the following five disk access requests of the form (request id, cylinder number) that are present in the disk scheduler queue at a given time.

(P, 155), (Q, 85), (R, 110), (S, 30), (T, 115)

Assume the head is positioned at cylinder 100. The scheduler follows Shortest Seek Time First scheduling to service the requests.

Which one of the following statements is FALSE?
options: Q is serviced after S, but before T.
The head reverses its direction of movement between servicing of Q and P.

solutionDiagram.alt: Head movement under shortest seek time first from cylinder 100: to R at 110, T at 115, Q at 85, S at 30 and P at 155, with the seek distances 10, 5, 30, 55 and 125.

steps.title: Cylinders, seek time and the SSTF rule
steps.body: A disk surface is divided into concentric tracks, called **cylinders** when stacked across platters. To serve a request the head must move to its cylinder; the **seek distance** is the difference of the two cylinder numbers, and seek time grows with it. **Shortest Seek Time First (SSTF)** has one rule: from the current head position, service the pending request whose cylinder is nearest. It does not care about direction. The head **reverses direction** when two consecutive moves go opposite ways.

steps.title: Run SSTF from cylinder 100
steps.body: Head at 100. Distances: R 10, Q 15, T 15, P 55, S 70. R is nearest: go to 110. Head at 110: T 5, Q 25, P 45, S 80, so T at 115. Head at 115: Q 30, P 40, S 85, so Q at 85. Head at 85: S 55, P 70, so S at 30. Last, P at 155. The service order is R, T, Q, S, P with moves 10, 5, 30, 55 and 125 cylinders. The first two moves go up, the next two down, the last up.

steps.title: Judge the four statements against the order R, T, Q, S, P
steps.body: A: T is served second and P is served last, so T comes before P. True. B: Q is served after T and before S, not after S. So "Q is serviced after S, but before T" is false. C: between Q and P the head goes down to S at 30 and then up to P at 155: it reverses at S. True. D: R is served first, before P. True. The FALSE statement is B.

shortcut.body: You only need the order. From 100 the nearest is R (10), then T (5). From 115 the choice is Q (30) against P (40): Q. Then S, then P. So Q is before S, and B, which says the opposite, is the false statement. About 1.5 minutes. Check that no step has a tie in distance (there is none), or the order would need a rule.

traps.text: T before P is true: T is served second and P last, because P is never the nearest pending request until it is the only one left. Choosing A usually means reading FALSE as TRUE; three of the four statements are true and the question wants the odd one.

Reversal between Q and P looks like it needs the head to hit an end of the disk. It does not: the head reverses whenever the next nearest request lies on the other side, here at S (down to 30, then up to 155).

R is the first request served, because it is only 10 away. Candidates who feel the head "should go down first" or who prefer the nearest in a fixed direction mark it false, but SSTF has no direction rule.

recognize.clues: The stem lists requests as (id, cylinder), gives the head position and names Shortest Seek Time First, so the service order comes from repeatedly taking the nearest pending cylinder.
recognize.contrast: Do not confuse it with SCAN or elevator scheduling. Those keep sweeping in one direction, while SSTF may reverse at any moment if the nearest request lies the other way.

check.body: Test statement B directly, without rerunning the order. The only cylinder below 85 is S at 30, and before Q is served the head can only stand at 100, 110, 115 or 155, all at or above 85. From every such position Q lies between the head and S, so Q is the nearer of the two and S can never be served first. That makes "Q is serviced after S" false whatever happens to P, R and T, so B is the false statement.

questions.stem:
Consider the following set of processes, assumed to have arrived at time 0. Consider the CPU scheduling algorithms Shortest Job First (SJF) and Round Robin (RR). For RR, assume that the processes are scheduled in the order $P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4$.

If the time quantum for RR is 4 ms, then the absolute value of the difference between the average turnaround times (in ms) of SJF and RR (round off to 2 decimal places) is ___________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Two Gantt charts. SJF: P3 0 to 2, P4 2 to 6, P2 6 to 13, P1 13 to 21. Round robin with quantum 4: P1 0 to 4, P2 4 to 8, P3 8 to 10, P4 10 to 14, P1 14 to 18, P2 18 to 21.

steps.title: Turnaround time, SJF and round robin
steps.body: **Turnaround time** is completion time minus arrival time; here every arrival time is 0, so it equals the completion time. **SJF** runs the shortest burst first and lets it finish (all arrive together, so preemption never matters). **Round robin** keeps a queue in the stated order P1, P2, P3, P4, runs the head for at most one quantum of 4 ms, and sends it to the back if it still needs the CPU. The question wants the absolute value of the difference of the two mean turnaround times.

steps.title: SJF
steps.body: Order by burst: P3 (2), P4 (4), P2 (7), P1 (8). Completion times: P3 at 2, P4 at 2 + 4 = 6, P2 at 6 + 7 = 13, P1 at 13 + 8 = 21. Mean turnaround = (2 + 6 + 13 + 21) / 4 = 42 / 4 = 10.5.

steps.title: Round robin, quantum 4
steps.body: 0 to 4: P1 runs, 4 left. 4 to 8: P2 runs, 3 left. 8 to 10: P3 runs its 2 and finishes at 10. 10 to 14: P4 runs its 4 and finishes at 14. 14 to 18: P1 runs its last 4, finishes at 18. 18 to 21: P2 runs its last 3 and finishes at 21. Completion times P1 18, P2 21, P3 10, P4 14. Mean turnaround = (18 + 21 + 10 + 14) / 4 = 63 / 4 = 15.75.

steps.title: Difference
steps.body: |10.5 - 15.75| = 5.25 ms, already at two decimal places.

shortcut.body: All arrivals are 0, so compare the sums of completion times: 42 for SJF and 63 for RR, a difference of 21 over 4 processes, 5.25. Using waiting times instead gives the same difference, because turnaround = waiting + burst and both algorithms run the same bursts. About 2 minutes. Unsafe if arrivals differ: turnaround is then completion minus arrival, not completion alone.

traps.text: Giving the difference of the totals, 21, rather than of the means. Both are averages over four processes; divide by 4.
Treating the quantum as 8 or more makes RR behave as FCFS: completion times 8, 15, 17, 21 and a mean turnaround of 15.25, so a difference of 4.75.
Reporting only one mean: 10.5 (SJF) or 15.75 (RR). The question asks for the absolute value of their difference.

recognize.clues: A time quantum of 4 ms and the instruction to schedule in the order P1 to P4 mark Round Robin; the same table is then run under SJF to compare average turnaround times.
recognize.contrast: SJF looks like Round Robin because both use the same burst table, but SJF never takes the CPU back from a running process and ignores queue order, while Round Robin cuts every process off after one quantum.

check.body: Use waiting time instead of turnaround time. SJF waits are 0, 2, 6 and 13, which sum to 21. Round Robin waits are completion minus burst: P1 10, P2 14, P3 8, P4 10, which sum to 42. Turnaround is waiting plus burst, and the bursts are the same in both, so the gap in the sums of waits must match the gap in the sums of turnarounds. Also SJF minimises the average, so the Round Robin mean must come out the larger, as it does.

questions.stem:
Consider the following four processes with arrival times (in milliseconds) and their length of CPU bursts (in milliseconds) as shown below:

These processes are run on a single processor using preemptive Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling algorithm. If the average waiting time of the processes is 1 millisecond, then the value of Z is________.

solutionDiagram.alt: SRTF Gantt chart for Z = 2: P1 runs 0 to 1, P2 1 to 2, P1 2 to 4, P4 4 to 6, P3 6 to 9, with the arrivals of P1 at 0, P2 at 1, P3 at 3 and P4 at 4 marked.

steps.title: Waiting time, SRTF, and what the question asks
steps.body: **Waiting time** of a process is completion minus arrival minus burst: the time it sits ready without running. **SRTF** (shortest remaining time first) is preemptive: at every arrival the scheduler runs whichever ready process has the least time still to run. Here the average waiting time is given (1 ms) and the unknown is a burst, Z. So the plan is to build the schedule, write the total wait as a function of Z, and solve. The total wait is $4 \times 1 = 4$ ms.

steps.title: The schedule up to time 4 does not depend on Z
steps.body: t = 0: P1 runs. t = 1: P2 arrives with burst 1, and P1 has 2 left, so P2 preempts and runs 1 to 2. t = 2: P1 resumes with 2 left. t = 3: P3 arrives with 3, but P1 has 1 left, so P1 continues and ends at 4. Waits so far: P1 = 4 - 0 - 3 = 1 and P2 = 2 - 1 - 1 = 0, which add to 1. At t = 4, P4 arrives and P1 is done, so only P3 (3) and P4 (Z) are left, with no later arrival.

steps.title: Two cases for Z, then solve
steps.body: P3 and P4 must therefore add up to a wait of $4 - 1 = 3$. Case $Z < 3$: P4 runs first at 4 and waits 0, then P3 runs from $4 + Z$ and waits $(4 + Z) - 3 = 1 + Z$. Setting $1 + Z = 3$ gives $Z = 2$, which is below 3, so the case is consistent. Case $Z \ge 3$: P3 runs first (it waits $4 - 3 = 1$) and P4 starts at 7 and waits $7 - 4 = 3$, a total of 4, not 3. So only $Z = 2$ works. A script that tries Z from 0.5 to 10 finds an average of 1 only at Z = 2.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: With Z = 2: P4 runs 4 to 6, P3 runs 6 to 9. Waits: P1 1, P2 0, P3 = 9 - 3 - 3 = 3, P4 = 6 - 4 - 2 = 0. Sum 4, mean 1. So Z = 2.

shortcut.body: Trace SRTF to t = 4 (P1 is preempted once, waits 1; P2 waits 0). Then it is a two-process SJF, P3 against P4, and the remaining wait must be 3. Try Z = 2: P4 first, P3 waits 3 (from 3 to 6). Total 4, mean 1. Try Z of 3 or more: total 5, too big. About 2 minutes. This works because Z is small enough to beat P3; the large case is easy to rule out as it always gives a total of 5 or more.

traps.text: Treating the algorithm as non-preemptive SJF. P2 then waits for P1 to finish (wait 2), and the same equation gives Z = 1. SRTF lets P2 preempt P1 at t = 1.

Forgetting P1's wait of 1 (it loses the CPU to P2 for 1 ms) sets the target for P3 and P4 at 4 instead of 3. Every Z of 3 or more meets that target, so the answer seems to be 3 or larger instead of 2.

recognize.clues: The words preemptive Shortest Remaining Time First, together with arrival times that differ, mean a newcomer can displace the running process, so remaining time is compared at every arrival.
recognize.contrast: Non-preemptive SJF compares only full bursts when the CPU is free, so P2 would wait for P1 to finish; in SRTF the comparison is made at each arrival, and P2 can preempt P1.

check.body: Test the neighbours of the result. With Z = 1, P4 runs 4 to 5 and P3 runs 5 to 8, so the waits are 1, 0, 2 and 0, a mean of 0.75. With Z = 3 or more, P3 runs first and the total wait rises to 5, a mean of 1.25. The mean moves from below 1 to above 1 as Z grows, and only the value between those two gives exactly 1.

questions.stem:
Consider a storage disk with 4 platters (numbered as 0, 1, 2 and 3), 200 cylinders (numbered as 0, 1, … , 199), and 256 sectors per track (numbered as 0, 1, … , 255). The following 6 disk requests of the form [sector number, cylinder number, platter number] are received by the disk controller at the same time:

[120, 72, 2] , [180, 134, 1] , [60, 20, 0] , [212, 86, 3] , [56, 116, 2] , [118, 16, 1]

Currently the head is positioned at sector number 100 of cylinder 80, and is moving towards higher cylinder numbers. The average power dissipation in moving the head over 100 cylinders is 20 milliwatts and for reversing the direction of the head movement once is 15 milliwatts. Power dissipation associated with rotational latency and switching of head between different platters is negligible.

The total power consumption in milliwatts to satisfy all of the above disk requests using the Shortest Seek Time First disk scheduling algorithm is _______.

solutionDiagram.alt: Head path under shortest seek time first from cylinder 80, moving up: 86, 72, 116, 134, 20, 16, with moves of 6, 14, 44, 18, 114 and 4 cylinders and direction reversals at 86, 72 and 134.

steps.title: What counts: cylinders and reversals
steps.body: Only the **cylinder** number matters here: sectors and platters cost no power, as the stem says. **SSTF** (shortest seek time first) always services the pending request whose cylinder is nearest to the head, whatever direction that is. The power has two parts. Moving the head costs 20 mW per 100 cylinders, so a total travel of $D$ cylinders costs $D / 100 \times 20$. Each **reversal** (a move in the opposite direction to the previous move) costs 15 mW. The head starts moving up, so a first move upward is not a reversal.

steps.title: Order of service under SSTF
steps.body: Requested cylinders: 72, 134, 20, 86, 116, 16. Head at 80: nearest is 86 (6 away, against 8 for 72), so go up to 86. From 86: 72 is 14 away, 116 is 30: go to 72. From 72: 116 is 44 away, 20 is 52: go to 116. From 116: 134 is 18, 20 is 96: go to 134. From 134: 20 is 114, 16 is 118: go to 20. Then 16. The path is 80, 86, 72, 116, 134, 20, 16; no step has a tie.

steps.title: Total distance and reversals
steps.body: Moves: 6 (up), 14 (down), 44 (up), 18 (up), 114 (down), 4 (down). Total distance $D = 6 + 14 + 44 + 18 + 114 + 4 = 200$ cylinders. Direction changes: the first move is up like the head's start (no reversal), then up to down at 86, down to up at 72, up to down at 134. So $r = 3$.

steps.title: Power
steps.body: Movement: $200 / 100 \times 20 = 40$ mW. Reversals: $3 \times 15 = 45$ mW. Total $40 + 45 = 85$ mW.

shortcut.body: Write only the cylinder order: 80, 86, 72, 116, 134, 20, 16. The distance is 200 (two units of 100, so 40 mW), and you count the direction changes along the path: up, down, up, up, down, down has three changes, 45 mW. Total 85. About 2.5 minutes. The head's initial direction matters for the first move only: if the nearest request were below, that first move would be a reversal.

traps.text: Counting only the movement power gives 40. The question adds a separate cost for each reversal, and SSTF has three.
Missing one of the three reversals (for example the one at 72, where the head turns up again) gives 70; counting an extra reversal at the start gives 100.
Choosing the next request by the "sector number" or "platter number" in each triple. Those cost nothing here; only the cylinder decides the order.

recognize.clues: The stem names Shortest Seek Time First and gives cylinder numbers, a start position and a direction, so the service order comes from always choosing the nearest cylinder, and the power cost counts distance and direction changes.
recognize.contrast: SCAN and LOOK sweep in one direction and turn only at the end, whereas SSTF may turn back at any moment toward whichever cylinder is nearest; that is why reversals have to be counted request by request.

check.body: Recompute the distance by splitting it by direction. Upward moves total 6 + 44 + 18 = 68 and downward moves total 14 + 114 + 4 = 132. The net displacement must equal the difference between the end and start cylinders, 16 - 80 = -64, and 68 - 132 = -64 agrees. The two parts add to the total distance, and the sequence of directions can be counted again from the signs of the moves.

questions.stem:
Consider the set of processes with arrival time (in milliseconds), CPU burst time (in milliseconds), and priority (0 is the highest priority) shown below. None of the processes have I/O burst time.

The average waiting time (in milliseconds) of all the processes using preemptive priority scheduling algorithm is ___________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Preemptive priority Gantt chart: P1 0 to 2, P4 2 to 5, P2 5 to 33, P4 33 to 40, P1 40 to 49, P3 49 to 51, P5 51 to 67, with arrivals and priorities marked above.

steps.title: Priority scheduling, preemption and waiting time
steps.body: In **priority scheduling** each process has a priority number, and here 0 is the best. The CPU always runs the ready process with the best (smallest) number. It is **preemptive** when a newly arrived process with a better priority than the running one takes the CPU at once, and the displaced process keeps the time it still needs and returns to the ready queue. The **waiting time** of a process is completion minus arrival minus burst: the time it spends ready but not running.

steps.title: Follow the arrivals in time order
steps.body: t = 0: only P1 (priority 2) is present, so it runs. t = 2: P4 (priority 1) arrives, better than 2, and P1 is preempted with 9 left. P4 runs from 2. t = 5: P2 (priority 0) arrives, the best of all, and P4 is preempted with 7 left. P2 runs 5 to 33 (28 units). While P2 runs, P5 (priority 4) arrives at 9 and P3 (priority 3) at 12, both worse than 0, so nothing changes.

steps.title: After P2 finishes at 33
steps.body: Ready: P1 (priority 2, 9 left), P4 (priority 1, 7 left), P3 (priority 3, 2), P5 (priority 4, 16). Best first: P4 runs 33 to 40, P1 runs 40 to 49, P3 runs 49 to 51, P5 runs 51 to 67. No later arrival exists, so nothing preempts.

steps.title: Waiting times and their mean

shortcut.body: Only two preemptions matter, at t = 2 and t = 5; after P2 the order is just by priority: P4, P1, P3, P5. The CPU is never idle, so the last completion is the total burst, 67. List the completions 49, 33, 51, 40, 67 and subtract arrival and burst for each: 38, 0, 37, 28, 42. Sum 145, mean 29. About 3 minutes.

traps.text: Using non-preemptive priority (P1 runs to 11, then P2, P4, P3, P5) gives 24.4. The question says preemptive.
Reading a larger number as a higher priority reverses every decision and gives 18.4. The stem says 0 is the highest priority.
Serving in order of arrival (FCFS) ignores the priorities and gives 23.6.

recognize.clues: Each process carries a priority number with 0 stated as the highest, and the stem says preemptive priority, so the best-numbered ready process runs and a better arrival interrupts.
recognize.contrast: SRTF also preempts, but it ranks by remaining time; here the burst length never decides who runs, only the priority number does.

check.body: Find each wait as the length of the gaps when the process is ready but off the CPU. P1 is ready from time 2 to 40, 38 ms. P4 arrives at 2, starts at once, is stopped at 5 and resumes at 33, so it waits 28 ms. P3 arrives at 12 and starts at 49, 37 ms. P5 arrives at 9 and starts at 51, 42 ms. P2 never waits. This uses gaps rather than completion times, and the CPU stays busy until the total burst of 67 ms.

questions.stem:
Consider the following CPU processes with arrival times (in milliseconds) and length of CPU bursts (in milliseconds) as given below :

If the pre-emptive shortest remaining time first scheduling algorithm is used to schedule the processes, then the average waiting time across all processes is __________ milliseconds.

solutionDiagram.alt: SRTF Gantt chart: P1 0 to 3, P2 3 to 6, P4 6 to 8, P1 8 to 12, P3 12 to 17, with arrivals P1 at 0, P2 at 3, P3 at 5 and P4 at 6 marked.

steps.title: Waiting time and the SRTF rule
steps.body: **Waiting time** is the time a process spends ready but not running: completion minus arrival minus burst. **SRTF** (shortest remaining time first) is preemptive: whenever a process arrives or finishes, the CPU goes to the ready process with the least time still to run. A newcomer whose burst is shorter than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

steps.title: Build the schedule event by event
steps.body: t = 0: P1 runs. t = 3: P2 arrives with 3; P1 has 4 left, so P2 preempts and runs 3 to 6. At t = 5, P3 arrives with 5, and P2 has 1 left, so P2 continues. At t = 6, P2 finishes and P4 arrives with 2. Ready: P1 with 4 left, P3 with 5, P4 with 2. P4 runs 6 to 8. At t = 8: P1 (4) beats P3 (5), so P1 runs 8 to 12. Last, P3 runs 12 to 17.

steps.title: Waits and the mean

shortcut.body: Only one preemption happens (P2 over P1 at t = 3); P4 at t = 6 arrives just as P2 ends, so it simply wins the choice. Order of running: P1, P2, P4, P1, P3. The completions 12, 6, 17, 8 minus arrival and burst give waits 5, 0, 7, 0, so the mean is 3. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Using non-preemptive SJF (P1 runs to 7, then P4, P2, P3) gives a mean of 3.5. SRTF lets P2 take the CPU at t = 3.
Serving in arrival order (FCFS) gives 4.5; the question names SRTF.
Computing turnaround time (completion minus arrival), which averages 7.25, instead of waiting time. Subtract the burst as well.

recognize.clues: Preemptive shortest remaining time first, plus arrival times spread between 0 and 6, means the remaining time of the running process is compared with every newcomer.
recognize.contrast: Plain SJF would let P1 finish its 7 ms before anyone else ran; the word preemptive is what allows P2 to take the CPU at time 3.

check.body: The CPU is never idle, so the last completion must equal the sum of all bursts, 7 + 3 + 5 + 2 = 17. Count each wait directly as the time spent ready but not running: P1 is off the CPU only while P2 and P4 run, which takes 5 ms, and P3 is ready from 5 and starts at 12, which takes 7 ms. P2 and P4 start the moment they arrive or get chosen after a short comparison, and wait 0.
